title: Celebrating Colleagues for Personal Milestones Can Establish a Dangerous Precedent
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article surfaces an uncomfortable tension: leaders want to celebrate team members' personal milestones, but formally sponsoring one celebration obligates them to do the same for everyone in the future or risk accusations of favoritism. The author walks through a concrete example, a leader-funded reception for one colleague's new baby, that leaves other new parents on the team feeling overlooked in the following months. The recommended solution isn't to withhold recognition altogether, but for leaders to step back from official sponsorship and let colleagues organize celebrations independently, with leaders free to attend as individuals rather than as organizational representatives. The piece frames this as a matter of fairness and long-term credibility.
points: Officially sponsoring one colleague's personal celebration sets a precedent to do the same for everyone
Team members who feel treated differently often stay silent, but the dissatisfaction can last for years
The fix: let colleagues organize celebrations themselves rather than the organization officially sponsoring them
Leaders can still personally attend as individuals, just not as official representatives of the team or organization
quotes: Once the organization, team, or leadership endorses, sponsors, or funds such an event, it becomes symbolic that they do so in the future for everyone with the same good or bad news.
Those who perceive that they’ve been treated differently will often keep it to themselves. But the taste of dissatisfaction often stays with them.
Good leaders don’t wash their hands of this dilemma by avoiding all recognition and celebration. Instead, they encourage others to arrange such celebrations on their own
The leaders, too, can partake in the event as long as they represent themselves and not the organization or team.
The best leaders believe everyone counts and prove it by the precedents they set or don’t.
